section.title: Final Exhortations and Greetings
section.sectionRationale: Having reordered the household under Christ, Paul turns the church outward and upward. He calls them to devote themselves to prayer, to watch and give thanks, and to pray for open doors for his own gospel proclamation even from prison. Their life before outsiders is to be wise and time-redeeming, their speech gracious and seasoned with salt. Then the letter fills with names: Tychicus and Onesimus who carry it, Aristarchus, Mark, Justus, Epaphras who wrestles in prayer, Luke, Demas, Nympha, Archippus. The great doctrine of the supremacy of Christ ends not in abstraction but in a living network of ordinary believers, some in chains, some serving quietly, all bound together in the Lord. Paul signs it in his own hand, asks them to remember his chains, and leaves them with grace.
section.thesis: The letter that soared to the heights of Christ's supremacy closes on its knees and among its friends: a church devoted to watchful, thankful prayer, wise and gracious toward outsiders, and embedded in a real fellowship of named co-workers through whom the gospel travels, sealed by Paul's own hand and the grace of Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the call to watchful prayer and wise, gracious witness (4:2-6); the sending of Tychicus and Onesimus with news and encouragement (4:7-9); greetings from a circle of fellow workers, with Epaphras wrestling in prayer (4:10-14); and the final instructions, the shared letter, the charge to Archippus, and Paul's own signature and closing grace (4:15-18).

units.label: Devotion to prayer and wise witness
units.note: watchful, thankful prayer, open doors, and gracious speech

verses.text: {{proskartereo|Devote yourselves}} to prayer, being watchful and thankful,
as you pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, so that we may proclaim the {{mysterion|mystery}} of Christ, for which I am in chains.
Pray that I may declare it clearly, as I should.
Act wisely toward outsiders, {{exagorazo|redeeming the time}}.
Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with {{halas|salt}}, so that you may know how to answer everyone.

units.label: Tychicus and Onesimus
units.note: news and encouragement carried by beloved brothers

verses.text: Tychicus will tell you all the news about me. He is a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a {{syndoulos|fellow servant}} in the Lord.
I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts.
With him I am sending Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you about everything here.

units.label: Greetings from fellow workers
units.note: a gospel embedded in a network of real people

verses.text: My fellow prisoner Aristarchus sends you greetings, as does Mark the cousin of Barnabas. You have already received instructions about him: If he comes to you, welcome him.
Jesus, who is called Justus, also sends greetings. These are the only Jews among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.

Epaphras, who is one of you and a servant of Christ Jesus, sends you greetings. He is always {{agonizomai|wrestling}} in prayer for you, so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God.
For I testify about him that he goes to great pains for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis.
Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas send you greetings.

units.label: Final instructions and Paul's own hand
units.note: the shared letter, the charge to Archippus, and the closing grace

verses.text: Greet the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha and the church that meets at her house.
After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.
Tell Archippus: "See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord."
This greeting is in my own hand, Paul. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.

proskartereo.gloss: To persist steadfastly, to attend constantly, to devote oneself to something with unwavering attention. Paul commands the Colossians to proskartereo in prayer: not to pray occasionally but to hold fast to it as a settled habit. The same verb describes the early church devoting themselves to the apostles' teaching and prayer in Acts, marking prayer as a persevering discipline rather than a passing impulse.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a truth once hidden and now revealed by God. For Paul the mystery is Christ Himself, and the gospel that Gentiles are fellow heirs in Him. Even in chains, Paul asks not for release but for open doors to proclaim this mystery clearly, showing that the revealed Christ, not the preacher's comfort, is the point of his imprisonment.

exagorazo.gloss: To buy up, to redeem, to purchase out of the marketplace. In the phrase redeeming the time it pictures believers buying up every opportunity, seizing the passing moment for good before it is lost. Paul uses the same verb elsewhere for Christ redeeming us from the curse of the law, so the believer's wise use of time echoes the costly redemption already accomplished for them.

halas.gloss: Salt, which preserves, purifies, and gives flavor. Speech seasoned with salt is speech that is wholesome and winsome, neither bland nor corrupt, carrying a grace that both preserves the hearer from decay and makes the truth appetizing. Jesus called His disciples the salt of the earth, and Paul applies the image to the ordinary conversations of Christians with outsiders.

syndoulos.gloss: A fellow slave, one who serves the same master alongside another. Paul calls Tychicus a syndoulos in the Lord, placing himself and his co-worker side by side as slaves of the one Master, Christ. The word quietly levels the ground: apostle and messenger alike are owned by and answerable to the same Lord they serve together.

agonizomai.gloss: To struggle, to contend, to labor as in an athletic contest or a battle; the root of the English word agonize. Epaphras is always agonizomai in prayer for the Colossians, wrestling on their behalf that they may stand mature and assured. The word shows that intercession is real work, a strenuous striving of love, not a casual afterthought.

basic.context: Paul brings the letter home. After lifting the church to see the supremacy of Christ and reordering their new life and their households, he now calls them to persevering, watchful, thankful prayer, and asks them to pray for him, that God would open doors for the gospel even while he sits in chains. He wants their public life to be wise toward outsiders and their speech gracious, seasoned with salt. Then he names his companions one by one: Tychicus and Onesimus carrying the letter, Aristarchus, Mark, Justus, Epaphras who wrestles in prayer, Luke and Demas, and the churches of Laodicea and Nympha's house. He signs the letter in his own hand, asks them to remember his chains, and closes with grace.
basic.hermeneutics: These closing verses mix direct commands (devote yourselves to prayer, act wisely, let your speech be gracious) with personal news and greetings. The commands are timeless instruction for the church; the greetings are historical, yet far from filler, they reveal how the gospel actually moved through a web of named, ordinary people. Read the imperatives as abiding calls and the names as evidence that Christ's mission is carried by real community, not by lone heroes.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul tells them to proskartereo in prayer, to hold fast to it steadfastly. He asks prayer that he might proclaim the mysterion, the once hidden and now revealed Christ. Believers are to be exagorazo, redeeming or buying up the time, and their speech is to be seasoned with halas, salt that preserves and flavors. Tychicus is a syndoulos, a fellow slave of the same Master, and Epaphras is always agonizomai, wrestling in prayer for them.
basic.typology: Paul's chains for the gospel foreshadow the pattern of the suffering servant of Christ, who fills up in his own body what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the church. The shared reading of letters between congregations anticipates the one universal church united by the apostolic word. Epaphras wrestling in prayer echoes the great intercessors of Scripture and points to Christ, our great High Priest who ever lives to intercede.
basic.christ: Christ remains the center even in the greetings. Prayer opens doors for the mystery of Christ; Tychicus is a fellow servant in the Lord; Epaphras is a servant of Christ Jesus; Archippus is charged to complete the ministry he received in the Lord; and the letter ends with the grace of Christ. Every relationship and task in this closing is defined by its connection to Him. The supreme Christ of chapter one is the same Lord under whom this ordinary fellowship lives and labors.
basic.god: God is the one who opens doors for the word, sovereign over Paul's imprisonment and over the advance of the gospel. He is the God whose full will Epaphras longs for the church to know and stand assured in, and the God whose grace crowns the letter's close. He works His purposes not around His people but through their prayers, their words, their journeys, and their care for one another.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 6, sent at the same time, gives a fuller call to pray at all times and to pray for Paul that he may boldly make known the mystery of the gospel. Philemon names many of the same companions, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke, and Demas, tying the letters together. Acts records Tychicus, Aristarchus, and Mark as Paul's travel companions.
basic.oneStory: The letter that began by declaring Christ the image of the invisible God, in whom all things hold together, ends among a handful of named believers praying, carrying letters, and remembering a prisoner's chains. This is how the kingdom advances: the cosmic Christ working through a real, praying, speaking, sending community, until the gospel fills the world and every open door leads more people to Him.

context.literary:
The closing is more carefully built than it first appears. It opens with a short run of commands in 4:2 to 6 that follow one thread, speech. Verses 2 to 4 are about speech directed to God (prayer) and about the speech that prayer is for (declaring the mystery clearly). Verses 5 and 6 are about speech directed to outsiders. The first command and the last both concern what comes out of the mouth, and the passage moves from the church's words to God, to the apostle's words to the world, to the church's words to its neighbors.

Then the letter changes register. Verses 7 to 9 are the sending of the messengers, verses 10 to 14 a list of greetings from named companions, verses 15 to 17 greetings and instructions from Paul to the churches around, and verse 18 the signature. The names are not scattered randomly. The first two are carriers, Tychicus and Onesimus. The next three, Aristarchus, Mark and Justus, are the Jewish believers, grouped by verse 11. Epaphras, Luke and Demas follow, and verse 14 puts the doctor and the later deserter together without comment. The list is arranged in groups by background and role, and it ends with the church in Laodicea, which points to the exchange of letters in verse 16.

Many details in the list link back to the opening of the letter. Epaphras, who brought the gospel in 1:7, is the one who now prays in 4:12. The mystery of Christ that is the burden of 1:26 and 27 and 2:2 is the content Paul asks to proclaim. The "my own hand" of verse 18 and the greeting "Grace be with you" answer the opening "Grace and peace to you," 1:2. The letter closes where it began, with grace, and with the community and its messengers.
context.historical:
Paul writes in chains, a fact he mentions in verses 3, 10, 18 and elsewhere. The place of his imprisonment is debated, and the options are Rome (Acts 28:30 and 31, two years of house arrest), Caesarea (Acts 24:23) and Ephesus (a possibility that rests on inference). The Roman option is the traditional one, and the mention of Aristarchus and Luke, who both sailed with Paul to Rome in Acts 27, fits it. The details do not change the message of the closing.

The geography of the names is useful. Tychicus came from the province of Asia, Acts 20:4, and carries both this letter and the one to the Ephesians, Ephesians 6:21. Onesimus is "one of you," a Colossian, and he is traveling home with Tychicus carrying the letter to Philemon as well. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with Paul in Ephesus and on the voyage to Rome, Acts 19:29 and 27:2. Mark is the cousin of Barnabas, a detail that explains his link with the first missionary journey, Acts 13:13, and the later quarrel in Acts 15:37 to 39. "You have already received instructions about him" shows that the church had been told in advance of his arrival, probably to reassure them that the old breach had been mended. Second Timothy 4:11 later calls Mark useful in the ministry.

Epaphras is said to labor for Laodicea and Hierapolis as well, which suggests that his work reached across the valley. The church in Laodicea, a larger and richer neighboring city, shared teaching and letters with Colossae, which is the setting of verse 16. Laodicea later receives a harsh letter of its own, Revelation 3:14 to 22. The church that meets in Nympha's house shows that the Christians gathered in private homes, as in Philemon 2, and that a woman could be the host and patron of a congregation.
context.canonical:
The closing of Colossians takes up several threads from Scripture. The call to prayer is rooted in the example of Jesus in Gethsemane, where He told His disciples to watch and pray so as not to enter temptation, Mark 14:38. The early church in Acts is a praying community, Acts 1:14, 2:42, 6:4, and Paul himself says elsewhere to pray without ceasing, 1 Thessalonians 5:17. The request for an open door has parallels in 1 Corinthians 16:9, 2 Corinthians 2:12 and Acts 14:27, where God opens doors for the gospel.

The command about salt looks back to Jesus' words that His disciples are the salt of the earth, Matthew 5:13, and to His call to have salt among themselves and be at peace, Mark 9:50. It sits beside the wisdom tradition on gracious speech, such as Proverbs 15:1 and 25:11. First Peter 3:15 gives a close parallel: be prepared to answer everyone, with gentleness and respect.

The closing greetings echo the same patterns elsewhere in Paul's letters. Philemon 23 and 24 names the same circle, Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke, and 2 Timothy 4:10 and 11 shows what became of two of them: Demas had left in love of this world and Mark was wanted as useful. The signature "in my own hand" recurs in 1 Corinthians 16:21 and 2 Thessalonians 3:17, where Paul explains that it marks his letters as genuine. The Laodicean connection returns in Revelation 1:11 and 3:14, which shows the church there still existed and still needed correction a generation later.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul intends the closing to complete the argument and not only to say goodbye. A letter that has insisted on the supremacy of Christ ends by showing what a church under that Lord does: it prays, it speaks well, it welcomes, it works together and it reads along with other churches. He wants the Colossians to see that the great claims of the letter have practical shape. Devotion to prayer keeps them from drifting back to the visions of chapter 2, and wisdom in speech keeps them from isolation among their neighbors.

He also wants them to know that the apostle depends on them. The request for prayer shows a man in prison who needs the church as much as it needs him, and who is eager for a clear voice, not safety. The greetings show the Colossians that they belong to a wide network and are not left alone with local teachers. Every name is a quiet argument against the lone-voice religion of the opposition: the gospel is carried by many hands, and the Christian life is life in company. The charge to Archippus is the single note of challenge, a reminder that ministry received must be finished.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 2 to 6 are commands for the whole church. Devote yourselves to prayer, act wisely toward outsiders, let your speech be gracious. These apply today without adjustment.

Verses 7 to 18 are largely description of historical persons and arrangements: who is traveling, who sends greetings, where a church meets, what letter is to be exchanged. They are not commands to copy, and it would be a mistake to read the details as rules, for instance to hold meetings in houses or to swap letters between churches. What they prescribe by implication is the spirit of the whole: honest news, mutual care, warm welcome and unashamed gratitude for co-workers. Two lines sit between the categories. "If he comes to you, welcome him," verse 10, is a command to the church about a particular person, but it shows a principle of restoring a person who has failed. "Tell Archippus" is a charge to a named man, though it speaks to every believer given a task.

The right way to read the lists of names is as evidence of how the church actually functioned. They show a mission staffed by Jews and Gentiles, by a physician, a prisoner and a runaway slave now called brother, and by a woman who hosts a church. They also record failure, since Demas is named without praise. The closing teaches by being real.

debates.question: What is the 'letter from Laodicea' in verse 16?

views.label: A lost letter of Paul
views.case: The simplest reading is that Paul wrote a separate letter to Laodicea, which has not survived. Paul wrote more letters than the New Testament preserves, as 1 Corinthians 5:9 mentions an earlier letter to Corinth. The phrase 'from Laodicea' most naturally means a letter that would arrive from there, one the Colossians were to borrow.

views.label: The letter we call Ephesians
views.case: Some ancient manuscripts of Ephesians lack the words 'in Ephesus' in 1:1, and the letter shares so much material with Colossians and was carried by the same man, Tychicus. Some hold that it was a circular letter to the churches of the region, and that the copy that reached the Lycus valley came by way of Laodicea.

views.label: The letter to Philemon
views.case: Another proposal is that the letter in question is Philemon, since Archippus, named in verse 17, appears in Philemon 2 and may have lived in Laodicea. The case is thin, because Philemon is a private note and the text speaks of a letter to be read aloud in the church.

debates.bearing: The identity does not alter the purpose of the instruction: the apostolic word was meant to be read and shared beyond a single congregation. The exchange shows that from the earliest years churches treated Paul's letters as a common treasury, and it reminds readers that Scripture is the product of a living network.

debates.question: What does 'redeeming the time' ask of believers?

views.label: Seize each opportunity for witness
views.case: The word translated time is kairos, the right or opportune moment, not chronos, the ticking of the clock. In context, with outsiders in view and a prayer for an open door, the phrase tells believers to make the most of every opening to speak and to act for Christ. The parallel in Ephesians 5:16 says 'because the days are evil.'

views.label: Use time wisely and without waste
views.case: The verb exagorazo means to buy up, to purchase out of the market. Many take the phrase in a broader sense: do not squander the short time given, but spend it in a way that counts for the gospel. This reading points to the shortness of life and the urgency of the age.

views.label: Buy back what is being lost
views.case: Some stress the commercial image and the cost implied, noting that the same verb is used of Christ's redemption in Galatians 3:13. They read the phrase as an invitation to take time out of the hands of the present evil age, perhaps at the price of comfort or convenience.

debates.bearing: The readings are not rivals. In both the context and the grammar, the aim is that nothing in the church's life with outsiders be wasted. Paul is asking for alertness and generosity with time, not for frantic busyness.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 begins with proskartereite, from a word that combines "toward" and "strength" and means to hold fast to something and stay with it. Luke uses it of the first believers in Acts 1:14, 2:42 and 6:4, and Paul uses it for prayer in Romans 12:12. It is a present imperative, so the call is for a continuing habit. The next participle, gregorountes, "being watchful," comes from the verb for staying awake. It is the word Jesus used in Gethsemane, Mark 14:38, where the disciples slept. To pray "watchfully" is to pray with the alertness the disciples lacked. The third element, en eucharistia, "with thanksgiving," finishes the picture: awake, steady, grateful.

In verse 3 the request is for a thyra tou logou, "a door for the word." The Greek genitive can be heard as a door that the word walks through. Paul also names the content as to mysterion tou Christou, the mystery of Christ, a key word of the letter, 1:26 and 27 and 2:2. The reason he gives, "for which I am in chains," uses the word desmoi, bonds. In verse 4 the phrase "as I should" translates dei, a verb of necessity. Paul is under divine compulsion to proclaim the mystery plainly; he asks that it come out phaneroso, "made visible," clear, not wrapped in the obscure talk of the visionary teachers.

Verse 5 says to walk in wisdom toward those outside, ton kairon exagorazomenoi, "buying up the opportune time." The word for time is kairos, the right moment. The verb exagorazo is the same verb that Paul uses for Christ's redeeming in Galatians 3:13 and 4:5, though in the middle voice here. In verse 6 speech is to be en chariti, "in grace," halati artymenos, "seasoned with salt." The verb artyo means to season or prepare, and halas is salt. Salt in the ancient world flavored and preserved food. The image asks that a Christian's words be neither bland nor bitter, and that they preserve rather than spoil. The final clause says that you may know how to answer each person, heni hekasto, one by one. Paul does not give a single formula; he asks for wisdom suited to each.

In verse 7 Tychicus is called agapetos adelphos, "beloved brother," pistos diakonos, "faithful minister," and syndoulos, "fellow slave," in the Lord. The last term is a compound of "with" and "slave," and Paul uses it of Epaphras in 1:7. It places both Paul and Tychicus on the same level as the Colossians, under one Master. Verse 8 says Tychicus will "encourage your hearts," a phrase that includes the verb parakaleo, to comfort and exhort together.

Verse 10 calls Aristarchus a synaichmalotos, "fellow prisoner," literally a fellow captive taken in war. Philemon 23 gives the same title to Epaphras. Whether the men took turns sharing Paul's confinement or the word is a figure for their service is not known. Mark is the anepsios of Barnabas, a word usually rendered cousin. Verse 12 describes Epaphras as agonizomenos, "wrestling" or "struggling," the verb of the athletic contest, from which comes the English "agony." Paul used the verb and the noun of his own labor in 1:29 and 2:1. The goal is that the Colossians "stand mature and fully assured," teleioi kai peplerophoremenoi. The second word, from plerophoreo, means to be fully convinced and is related to Romans 4:21 and 14:5. It is the opposite of the doubt that the visionary teaching bred.

typology.type: Jesus in Gethsemane, the model of watchful prayer, Mark 14:34-38
typology.fulfillment: In Gethsemane Jesus asked His disciples to stay awake and pray, and they slept; He alone prayed through the hour of trial. Paul's call to be 'watchful' in prayer takes the failure of the disciples as the contrast. The correspondence is of the vigilant prayer that faces temptation. The escalation is that believers do not pray alone: Christ 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25, and the Spirit and Son stand with them, Romans 8:34. The pattern falls short in that Jesus faced the cup in a way no disciple can, and the church's watchfulness depends on His having done so.

typology.type: Paul's chains, the suffering of the servant, Colossians 1:24 and 4:18
typology.fulfillment: Paul's imprisonment for the gospel follows the pattern of the suffering of the righteous servant, and in 1:24 he says he completes in his own flesh what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the church. His request that they 'remember my chains' joins his cost to Christ's. The correspondence lies in vicarious service: his sufferings serve others, Philippians 1:12 to 14, 2 Timothy 2:9. The pattern is only a pattern, because Christ's afflictions are complete in the matter of atonement, while Paul's share in the suffering that goes with proclaiming that atonement.

Scripture preserves a line of intercessors, Moses on the mountain, Samuel for Israel, the priest bearing names on his breast. Epaphras wrestles for a church he may not be able to visit. The pattern reaches its center in Christ, who intercedes at God's right hand, Romans 8:34. The correspondence is of one who carries a people into God's presence. Epaphras's prayer is real but derivative, and its aim, 'mature and fully assured,' is what Christ's own intercession secures, Hebrews 7:25.

typology.type: Mark, the failed servant restored, Acts 15:37-39 and Colossians 4:10
typology.fulfillment: Mark deserted the first mission in Pamphylia, and Paul refused to take him again, to the point of a break with Barnabas. Here Mark is a comfort, and the church is told to welcome him. The pattern is of failure and restoration, the same pattern as Peter's after the denial, John 21:15 to 17. The correspondence is of grace that restores a servant. In 2 Timothy 4:11 Paul asks for Mark because he is useful. The story shows the gospel's work on its own workers, though it also records the cost of the break, which was not undone by the restoration.

study.christ:
Christ does not appear in the closing as a topic. He appears as the setting, the term by which every person and act is described. The mystery that Paul wants to declare is "the mystery of Christ," verse 3, which is the content of his preaching and the reason for his chains. In 1:27 the mystery is "Christ in you, the hope of glory," and in 2:2 it is "namely Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." The request for an open door is a request for opportunity to speak of Him.

Believers are people who are "in the Lord." Tychicus is a fellow servant in the Lord, Epaphras is a servant of Christ Jesus, Archippus received his ministry in the Lord, and even Paul's own signature is attached to the grace of the same Lord. The vocabulary is a catalogue of union. Each friend is named in terms of belonging to the same Master, and Paul's frequent use of "fellow" words, fellow servant, fellow prisoner, fellow worker, assumes a common Lord who binds them.

The passage also presents Him as the Lord who builds a people of many kinds. Verse 11 notes that the three Jewish believers named are among the only Jews who were fellow workers for the kingdom of God. The rest of the circle includes Gentiles, a Colossian who was once a slave, a physician, and a woman who hosts a church. The picture matches 3:11. In Christ the old divisions do not count, and the cooperation of this mixed company is a living picture of His reconciling work, 1:20 to 22.

His intercession gives Epaphras's wrestling its meaning. The prayer that the Colossians would stand mature and assured is what Christ, who is always interceding, desires for them, Romans 8:34 and Hebrews 7:25. We should not turn each name into a type of Christ, which would be forced, but the pattern is simple and firm: He is the center of a community that prays, speaks and works because of Him.

The letter ends with "Grace be with you." Grace is a person's gift, and in Paul's usage it is the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. The one who is supreme over creation and church, who reconciled all things by the blood of His cross, 1:15 to 20, closes the letter by giving Himself in grace.
study.god:
The God of the closing is the God who opens doors. Paul does not plan the progress of the gospel; he asks for prayer that God would open a door, which is a confession that the work depends on God. This coincides with Acts 14:27 and 1 Corinthians 16:9, where the same image describes God's initiative in sending the word forward. The imprisoned apostle does not say that the gospel is shut up with him. He presumes that the God who opens will open.

He is also a God who hears persistent prayer. The commands to devote oneself to prayer and to stay watchful assume that prayer matters, that what is asked of God changes what happens. Epaphras's wrestling rests on the assurance that God is able to make His people stand mature and assured in His whole will. The phrase "the full will of God" shows that God has a purpose for the Colossians and does not leave it to chance.

He is the God who keeps His people through different hands. The messengers, the co-workers, the hosts and the intercessors all serve a purpose that is not theirs. In 4:11 the circle is called "my fellow workers for the kingdom of God," a phrase that places even prison correspondence inside the rule of God. His work moves through letters, journeys, a physician's care and the hospitality of a household, so that no task is too ordinary.

The passage gives an account of God who forgives and restores people. Mark's inclusion shows a God whose restoring work extends to those who once failed, and Demas, who is named without comment, is a reminder that He does not coerce loyalty. Together they hold the tension between God's keeping and human responsibility, which the Bible does not resolve in a formula, 2 Timothy 4:10 and 11.

The doctrine of God here shapes worship at the point of thanksgiving. Prayer is to be in thanksgiving, verse 2. It matters because a God who gives is not only a source of needs to be met but a person to be honored. Speech that is "gracious" mirrors Him, since God speaks to people with grace. The final word of the letter, grace, completes the picture: He is the one from whom all the church's gifts, its messengers and its prayer, come as free gifts.

crossReferences.note: Pray in the Spirit at all times, and pray that Paul would boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, for which he is an ambassador in chains. It is the sister to Colossians 4:2 to 4, written about the same time. Reading them together shows that the request for prayer was close to the center of Paul's mind in prison.

Jesus finds His disciples asleep and tells them to watch and pray. The verb 'watch' is the one used in Colossians 4:2. Paul asks the Colossians to succeed where the disciples failed, and he places the prayer life of the church in the shadow of Gethsemane.

'A great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me.' Paul sees open doors and opposition together. The same phrase in Colossians 4:3 shows that his request is a request for opportunity, not comfort, and it frames the chains of the same verse as a challenge, not a cause for retreat.

'Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.' It is the same phrase as Colossians 4:5, with its reason given. The days are evil, so each opportunity is precious. The two letters together show that the call is not to anxiety but to wise use of each opening.

Be prepared to answer everyone who asks for the reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect. It matches Colossians 4:5 and 6 in aim and tone, and it fills out what 'know how to answer everyone' means. Witness is a reply to the questions of outsiders, given in a gracious manner.

The same circle sends greetings: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke. The matching names show that the two letters were written and sent together, and they let us put the Colossian household in context, since Onesimus was carrying both.

Demas, who loved this world, has left, and Mark is wanted as useful for the ministry. The two men named together here in Colossians 4:10 and 14 are seen years later on opposite roads. The passage keeps the greetings from sounding naive: faithfulness has to be kept up.

The sharp dispute between Paul and Barnabas over Mark, who had deserted them in Pamphylia. It gives the background to 'welcome him' in Colossians 4:10, and it shows how remarkable it is to find Mark in the apostle's circle, named as a comfort.

Lists Paul's companions, including Aristarchus and Tychicus from Asia. It confirms that the men of Colossians 4:7 and 10 were long-standing partners, and it shows the pattern of a mission carried out by a team from many places.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. The verb is the same one Paul uses in the phrase for redeeming the time in Colossians 4:5. The link is a reminder that the believer's use of time rests on a redemption that has already cost something.

'This greeting is in my own hand.' Paul writes the last words himself, as in 2 Thessalonians 3:17, where he says that this is his mark in every letter. The signature in Colossians 4:18 shows that he took personal responsibility for a letter written through a secretary.

Laodicea, the neighbor mentioned in Colossians 4:13, 15 and 16, later receives a rebuke from the risen Christ for being lukewarm. Seen beside the warm greetings of Colossians, it shows how a church can lose its first devotion, and it makes Epaphras's prayers for the whole valley more pressing.

study.oneStory:
The closing answers a question that goes back to Genesis: how will the blessing promised to the nations reach them? God told Abraham in Genesis 12:3 that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him. The long story of Israel kept the promise alive while seldom carrying it beyond its borders. In Colossians the promise is visible in the humblest form. A gospel that was once held in one nation is now carried by letters and messengers between Greek cities, passed on by a physician, a runaway slave, a woman with a spare room and a prisoner who asks for prayer.

The passage also answers the problem of Genesis 11. At Babel the nations were scattered and speech divided them. Here people of different origins are working side by side, and words that once divided are now used to bear one message. The command that speech be gracious and seasoned with salt belongs to the same story: speech, which humanity abused at Babel, is being redeemed.

In redemption's order the passage sits after the cross and before the end. The mystery of Christ has been revealed, 1:26, and the task now is to proclaim it. The chains show that the world resists, and the open door shows that God still works. This is the time between, and the church's calling in this time is simple: to pray, to speak wisely, to welcome one another, to complete the work given to each.

What the closing sets up beyond the letter is the church's life in the following decades, in which letters would be exchanged and a canon formed. Verse 16, the sharing of the letters between congregations, is the first small step of that process. It also sets up the failures of later years, since Demas leaves and Laodicea cools, and the warnings of Revelation are the sequel.

The story ends in the new creation, where the mystery is no longer hidden or proclaimed under pressure. People from every nation stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9, the prisoner is free, the watching is over, and the God who opened doors on earth opens the gates of the city. The grace with which the letter ends is the grace in which the story ends, for the One who is supreme over all things will give Himself to His people forever, as Revelation 21:3 describes.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the prayer he calls the Colossians to?

options.text: Devoted and persevering, being watchful and thankful.
options.note: Verse 2 calls for steadfast, alert, grateful prayer, not occasional prayer.

options.text: Occasional, only when a crisis arises.
options.note: The verb means to devote oneself steadfastly, a settled habit, not crisis prayer.

options.text: Silent and private, never for others.
options.note: Paul immediately asks them to pray for him and his mission.

options.text: Unnecessary, since God already knows their needs.
options.note: Paul explicitly commands them to devote themselves to prayer.

quiz.q: What does Paul ask the church to pray for on his behalf?

options.text: That God would open a door for the word so he can proclaim the mystery of Christ clearly.
options.note: Verses 3 and 4 show Paul's concern is gospel proclamation, not personal relief.

options.text: That he would be released from prison quickly.
options.note: Paul asks for open doors for the gospel, not first for his own freedom.

options.text: That his enemies would be punished.
options.note: His request is for clarity in preaching Christ, not vengeance.

options.text: That he would become famous among the churches.
options.note: His aim is the clear proclamation of Christ, not personal renown.

quiz.q: How should believers speak toward outsiders?

options.text: Graciously, seasoned with salt, ready to answer everyone.
options.note: Verse 6 calls for wholesome, winsome speech that answers wisely.

options.text: Bluntly, without regard for how it lands.
options.note: Speech is to be gracious and seasoned, not careless.

options.text: Only about religious topics, never ordinary matters.
options.note: The call is that all speech be gracious, not that it be narrowly religious.

options.text: As little as possible, to avoid trouble.
options.note: Paul assumes engagement with outsiders, answering everyone wisely.

quiz.q: What does Paul say Epaphras does for the Colossians?

options.text: He is always wrestling in prayer that they may stand mature and fully assured.
options.note: Verse 12 shows intercession as strenuous, loving labor for their maturity.

options.text: He collects money from them for Paul.
options.note: Epaphras labors in prayer for them, not in fundraising.

options.text: He teaches them a secret philosophy.
options.note: He is a servant of Christ who prays for their assurance in God's will.

options.text: He has abandoned them in their trouble.
options.note: He goes to great pains and wrestles in prayer for them.

quiz.q: How does Paul close the letter?

options.text: In his own hand, asking them to remember his chains, and leaving them with grace.
options.note: Verse 18 seals the letter personally and ends with the grace of Christ.

options.text: With a warning that he never wants to hear from them again.
options.note: He closes with warmth, remembrance, and grace, not rejection.

options.text: By demanding immediate payment for his ministry.
options.note: He asks them to remember his chains and blesses them with grace.

options.text: Without any personal word at all.
options.note: He signs it in his own hand, a deeply personal closing.

questions: Paul tells the church to devote themselves to prayer, watchful and thankful. What would it take for prayer to move from an occasional impulse to a steadfast habit in your life?
Even in chains, Paul asks for prayer for open doors to preach Christ, not first for his own release. How does that reorder what you tend to pray for yourself?
Your speech is to be gracious and seasoned with salt so you know how to answer everyone. Where do your ordinary conversations with outsiders need more grace, and where more salt?
Epaphras wrestled in prayer for people to stand mature and assured. Who are you willing to labor in prayer for like that, and what would that wrestling look like this week?
The letter ends among named, ordinary co-workers carrying the gospel together. Who are the people God has placed around you in the work of the gospel, and how could you encourage one of them?

translationNotes.note: Devote yourselves renders proskartereo, to persist steadfastly and attend constantly; it pictures prayer as a persevering discipline, the same devotion Acts ascribes to the first believers.
Redeeming the time translates exagorazo with kairos, buying up the opportune moment; believers are to seize every passing opportunity for good, as those already bought by Christ.
Seasoned with salt uses halas; wholesome, winsome speech that preserves and flavors, neither bland nor corrupt, echoing Jesus' image of His disciples as the salt of the earth.
This greeting is in my own hand marks Paul taking the pen from his scribe to authenticate the letter.
